elements.name: Message
elements.what: A discrete, self-contained packet of data (header plus body) exchanged between decoupled parts of a program through a channel rather than by direct call.
elements.problem: Two components need to exchange information without sharing call stacks, timing, or memory layout; packaging data as an addressable unit lets it be queued, routed, stored, and retried independently of sender and receiver.

elements.name: Message Queue
elements.what: A queue-backed channel on which producers enqueue messages and exactly one consumer dequeues each message, decoupling sender and receiver in time.
elements.problem: A producer must hand work or data to a consumer that runs at a different rate or on a different thread; queuing absorbs bursts and guarantees each message is processed once by one receiver.

elements.name: Publish-Subscribe Channel
elements.what: A channel that delivers a copy of each published message to every currently subscribed consumer instead of to a single receiver.
elements.problem: One event must reach an open-ended set of interested parties without the publisher knowing who they are; the channel handles fan-out so subscribers can be added or removed independently.
elements.borderline: Publish-subscribe as a system-wide architecture style is Phase 3 territory; this entry is the in-process/inter-thread channel mechanism (in-proc topics, broadcast queues).

elements.name: Correlation Identifier
elements.what: A unique identifier stamped on a request message and copied into its reply so the requester can match responses to outstanding requests.
elements.problem: With asynchronous request handling, replies arrive out of order and interleaved; without a carried token the requester cannot tell which reply answers which request.

elements.name: Request-Reply
elements.what: A two-message exchange in which a requester sends a message on one channel and the replier sends a response message back on another, layering call semantics over one-way messaging.
elements.problem: Messaging is inherently one-way, but many interactions need an answer; pairing a request channel with a reply channel restores the ask-and-answer conversation without blocking the transport.

elements.name: Return Address
elements.what: A field in the request message telling the replier which channel to send the reply on.
elements.problem: A replier serving many requesters cannot hard-code where responses go; carrying the reply channel in the message lets each requester receive its own answers.

elements.name: Message Filter
elements.what: A routing component that inspects each incoming message and passes it on only if it meets specified criteria, silently discarding the rest.
elements.problem: A consumer receives a broader stream than it wants; filtering at the channel keeps unwanted traffic from reaching downstream logic.

elements.name: Content-Based Router
elements.what: A router that examines message content and forwards each message to one of several output channels based on data-driven conditions.
elements.problem: Different messages in one stream must be handled by different processors; routing on content keeps senders ignorant of the receiver taxonomy.

elements.name: Splitter
elements.what: A component that breaks a composite message into a series of individual messages, each processable on its own.
elements.problem: A single message containing repeating elements (an order with many line items) must be handled per element; splitting lets each part flow through the pipeline independently.

elements.name: Aggregator
elements.what: A stateful component that collects correlated messages until a completeness condition holds, then publishes a single combined message.
elements.problem: Results that were split or produced in parallel must be recombined; the aggregator manages correlation, partial state, and completion/timeout rules.

elements.name: Resequencer
elements.what: A stateful buffer that holds out-of-order messages and releases them downstream in the correct sequence based on a sequence number.
elements.problem: Parallel processing or unordered channels scramble message order while consumers require it; buffering until gaps fill restores order without blocking the producers.

elements.name: Dead Letter Channel
elements.what: A designated channel to which the messaging layer moves messages that cannot be delivered or processed, instead of dropping or endlessly retrying them.
elements.problem: Undeliverable or repeatedly failing messages would otherwise poison the main queue or vanish silently; parking them aside preserves them for inspection and keeps the main flow healthy.

elements.name: Idempotent Receiver
elements.what: A consumer designed so that processing the same message more than once has the same effect as processing it once, typically by tracking already-seen message identifiers.
elements.problem: At-least-once delivery and retry produce duplicates; making the receiver duplicate-safe is cheaper and more robust than trying to guarantee exactly-once transport.

elements.name: Claim Check
elements.what: Store a message's bulky payload in a shared data store and pass only a key (the claim check) through the channel; the consumer redeems the key to retrieve the data.
elements.problem: Large payloads clog channels and intermediate processors that only need headers; moving the body out of band keeps messages small without losing access to the full data.

elements.name: Competing Consumers
elements.what: Multiple concurrent consumers receive from the same point-to-point channel, each message going to exactly one of them, so throughput scales with consumer count.
elements.problem: A single consumer cannot keep up with message arrival rate; letting a pool of consumers race for messages parallelizes processing while the queue preserves once-only delivery.

elements.name: Message Dispatcher
elements.what: A single consumer that receives messages from a channel and distributes each to one of several performers (typically worker threads) it coordinates.
elements.problem: When consumers must not compete directly (ordering, channel limitations, or work-assignment logic), one dispatcher can centralize receipt and delegate processing while still exploiting parallelism.

elements.name: Selective Consumer
elements.what: A consumer that applies a selection predicate so it receives only the subset of a channel's messages it is interested in, leaving the rest for other consumers.
elements.problem: Several consumer types share one channel but each handles only certain messages; consumer-side selection avoids either exploding the channel count or processing-and-discarding.

elements.name: Polling Consumer
elements.what: A consumer that explicitly asks the channel for a message when it is ready to process one, blocking or returning empty if none is available.
elements.problem: The application must control when and at what rate messages are consumed (e.g., single-threaded loops, rate limiting); pull-based receipt keeps consumption on the consumer's schedule.

elements.name: Event-Driven Consumer
elements.what: A consumer whose message-handling callback is invoked by the messaging layer as soon as a message arrives, rather than the consumer polling for it.
elements.problem: Polling wastes cycles and adds latency when messages are sporadic; inverting control lets messages be processed immediately with no busy-waiting.

elements.name: Message Expiration
elements.what: A timestamp or time-to-live stamped on a message after which the messaging layer or consumer treats it as stale and discards or dead-letters it instead of processing it.
elements.problem: Some data is only useful for a bounded time (quotes, sensor readings); expiration prevents consumers from acting on obsolete messages that queued up during delays.

elements.name: Wire Tap
elements.what: A fixed component inserted into a channel that forwards each message unchanged to the main destination while also copying it to a secondary channel for inspection, logging, or analysis.
elements.problem: You need to observe traffic on a point-to-point channel (debugging, auditing) without disturbing the primary flow or modifying sender/receiver.
elements.borderline: Commonly deployed as integration infrastructure, but equally implementable inside one in-process pipeline; kept IN as an observation mechanism, altitude-contested.

elements.name: Scatter-Gather
elements.what: Broadcast a request to multiple recipients, then use an aggregator to collect and combine their replies into a single response message.
elements.problem: One question has several potential answerers (best quote, parallel sub-computations); fan-out plus reply aggregation gets all answers concurrently and reduces them to one result.
elements.borderline: Named for cross-system integration, but recurs as an in-process fan-out/fan-in composite (parallel dispatch + join); altitude-contested, kept IN.

elements.name: Event Aggregator
elements.what: A single in-process object that registers for events from many sources and lets clients subscribe once with it, channeling and optionally generalizing all events to interested observers.
elements.problem: With many event sources, requiring each observer to find and register with every source explodes coupling and complicates observer lifetime management; a central aggregator makes registration one-stop and eases memory management of observers.

elements.name: Mailbox
elements.what: A per-receiver message deposit point - in RTOS kernels a one-message (or small) exchange object a task pends on; in actor systems the queue holding all messages addressed to one actor.
elements.problem: A task or actor needs a private, addressable place where others can leave messages for it to consume on its own schedule, decoupling sender timing from receiver processing.
elements.named_in: MicroC/OS-III: The Real-Time Kernel (and MicroC/OS-II message mailboxes) - Jean J. Labrosse (2009)

parked_architecture.name: Message Broker
parked_architecture.why: Central intermediary topology that decouples all senders from all receivers system-wide (EIP); primarily a statement of system-level structure.

parked_architecture.name: Message Bus
parked_architecture.why: Shared enterprise-wide bus connecting many applications via common channels and data model (EIP); an architecture style, not an in-process mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Channel Adapter
parked_architecture.why: Connects an application that was not built for messaging to the messaging infrastructure (EIP); a system-integration topology element.

parked_architecture.name: Messaging Bridge
parked_architecture.why: Connects two separate messaging systems so messages flow between them (EIP); inter-system topology.

parked_architecture.name: Pipes and Filters (integration style)
parked_architecture.why: As EIP presents it: system-level composition of processing steps connected by channels; the in-process pipeline/pipes-and-filters idiom is a distinct design-level element for the concurrency/POSA scout.

parked_architecture.name: Process Manager
parked_architecture.why: Central workflow/orchestration engine maintaining process state across multi-step message flows (EIP); system-level control structure.

parked_architecture.name: Routing Slip
parked_architecture.why: Itinerary attached to a message driving it through a system-level sequence of processing steps (EIP); trends architectural (dynamic workflow across components).

parked_architecture.name: Control Bus
parked_architecture.why: Separate management/monitoring channel overlay for administering a distributed messaging system (EIP system management); operations topology.

parked_architecture.name: Canonical Data Model
parked_architecture.why: Enterprise-wide agreement on a common data format to minimize translator count (EIP); cross-system data governance, not an implementable mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Guaranteed Delivery
parked_architecture.why: Persistence-backed delivery quality-of-service of the messaging infrastructure (EIP); a system-level guarantee rather than an in-process mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Durable Subscriber
parked_architecture.why: Subscription persistence so a disconnected subscriber misses no messages (EIP); a QoS feature of messaging infrastructure.

parked_architecture.name: Datatype Channel
parked_architecture.why: Channel-per-datatype organization convention for a messaging system (EIP); a channel-topology design decision, not a mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Integration Styles (File Transfer, Shared Database, Remote Procedure Invocation, Messaging)
parked_architecture.why: EIP's root-level styles for connecting applications; pure architecture-realm vocabulary for Phase 3.

excluded_notable.name: Command Message / Document Message / Event Message
excluded_notable.why: EIP's message-intent taxonomy; sub-classifications of Message folded into the message entry's aka rather than three separate elements.

excluded_notable.name: Message Sequence
excluded_notable.why: EIP construction pattern for multi-part transmission via sequence numbering; below charter granularity here, but sequence numbering itself may merit an element under a serialization-framing scout.

excluded_notable.name: Format Indicator
excluded_notable.why: A version/format field convention inside a message; below element granularity.

excluded_notable.name: Invalid Message Channel
excluded_notable.why: At this altitude the same mechanism as Dead Letter Channel (side channel for bad messages); EIP distinguishes only the cause (malformed vs undeliverable/expired).

excluded_notable.name: Message Translator, Envelope Wrapper, Content Enricher, Content Filter, Normalizer
excluded_notable.why: EIP message-transformation family; integration-side restatements of adapter/mapping/serialization concerns owned by other scouts' axes.

excluded_notable.name: Recipient List, Dynamic Router, Composed Message Processor
excluded_notable.why: EIP routing variants beyond the charter's in-process subset; mechanisms are compositions/variants of Content-Based Router + Splitter/Aggregator already cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: Messaging Gateway, Messaging Mapper, Service Activator, Transactional Client
excluded_notable.why: Messaging-endpoint API-shape patterns (gateway/mapper/adapter family); construction-api territory better owned by the Fowler PoEAA / API-shape scout.

excluded_notable.name: Detour, Smart Proxy, Message History, Message Store, Test Message, Channel Purger
excluded_notable.why: EIP system-management instrumentation for operating a messaging system; operational/practice-level rather than in-process design mechanisms (Wire Tap, the one with clear in-process recurrence, was kept IN).

excluded_notable.name: Message Channel, Message Router, Message Endpoint
excluded_notable.why: EIP root generalizations; the concrete specializations (point-to-point, pub-sub, content-based router, consumers) are cataloged instead of the abstract parents.

notes: Full EIP catalog (all 65 patterns) loaded live from enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/toc.html and triaged pattern-by-pattern: 22 EIP patterns pass the altitude test as in-process/inter-thread mechanisms (charter's 18 plus Message Expiration, Message Dispatcher, Wire Tap, Scatter-Gather - the latter two tagged borderline), 13 parked to architecture, the rest recorded as excluded_notable with fold rationale - nothing silently dropped. In-process eventing covered by Event Aggregator (Fowler eaaDev page loaded live; event bus folded as aka) and Mailbox (RTOS sense via Labrosse MicroC/OS, corpus id labrosse; actor mailbox folded as aka). Thin spots: (1) actor-model messaging vocabulary beyond mailbox (actor, ask/tell, become) not enumerated - likely the concurrency scout's territory; (2) signals/slots and delegate/event language mechanisms deliberately left to language-idiom scouts; (3) sequence numbering / framing mechanisms flagged in excluded_notable for the serialization-framing axis; (4) backpressure-aware channels (bounded queue semantics) assumed owned by the data-flow-buffering scout.
